subject: Question - multinomial with partially observed data

messages.author: 3e911bc3bc76c82d
messages.subject: Question - multinomial with partially observed data
parts:
Hi all!

This might be rather a simple question, but any feedback would be appreciated. 

Is there any way to model incomplete data in NIMBLE using a multinomial distribution? 
My study case is an animal that moves unidirectionally into binned distances, and these distance unit get discrete values between 1 and 11. However, for some individuals the distance is observed and for some it is not. Therefore, I end up having a vector that is a combination of discrete values between 1 and 11 and unobserved values ("NA"). My vector would be something like "NA NA 1 6 3 1 1 2 10 NA 1 NA 3 NA NA NA 4".

I would like to model this data using a multinomial distribution, so that based on the observed data I can infer values for those individuals in which it is unobserved. I have tried some approaches to do so but so far it does not work. I also do know that it was not possible to model a partially observed multinomial distribution in JAGS, and I still do not know if the problem is still present on NIMBLE. 

Does any of you guys have any idea about this? Is there a way to model it?

Thank you in advance!

Jaume

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: Question - multinomial with partially observed data
parts:
Hi Jaume,

If I understand correctly, the distribution for each individual animal is categorical, so I think you could assign "dcat" to each individual within a for loop, e.g.,:

for(i in 1:n)
   y[i] ~ dcat(p[1:K])

Then when setting the data vector for the variable 'y', you can specify some values as NA and those elements of the  variable will not be flagged as being data and MCMC sampers will by default be assigned to those elements.

-chris

parts:
Hi guys,

Coming back to my first question, I have a second question about an error I am getting. Sorry I thought it was already solved. 

So I basically inferred values based on a categorical in my vector of binned distances (1 NA 5 NA 3 4 1 1 NA NA NA...) and it worked well. 

for( i in 1:nind){
y[i] ~ dcat(pi[1:11])
}

pi[1:11] ~ ddirch(alpha[1:11])

I performed this separately and everything fine. Now I have to incorporate this vector as a dynamic index for a covariate to estimate a recapture probability, and perhaps here is where the problem comes. 

for( i in 1:nind){

logit(pT[i]) <- intercept + slope * (sampeff[y[i]])

}

In which sampeff is basically a vector with different sampling efforts (length = 11), and I am interested in getting the sampling effort value depending on the distance of every individual.

I would expect the model to run with no problems but I am being spammed this error when running nimbleModel:

"Warning: dynamic index out of bounds: expit(intercept[1] + slope[1] * (sampeff[y[i]]))"

Which is like if the binned distance object "y" was showing a value that is out of bounds for the sampling effort "sampeff" vector, right? I cannot understand why I get this if both vectors have the same range of values and NAs should be already gone. 

Any ideas about this? Perhaps there's a misconception from my side on how the model is working?

Thanks again! 

Jaume

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: Question - multinomial with partially observed data
parts:
Hi Jaume,

If you don't provide initial values for the NA elements, then that's just nimble warning you (it's not an error) that it can't do model calculations for pT because there are y[i] values that are missing.  Some solutions:

1) You can provide initial values for the NA elements via 'inits', e.g.,

nimbleModel(code, data = list(y = c(7, NA, 3)), inits = list(y = c(NA, 5, NA))

2) You can avoid having nimbleModel run calculate on the model by passing "calculate=FALSE" as an argument to nimbleModel. This will suppress the warning.

3) You can ignore the warning and just let nimble generate initial values for the NA elements. Often it is a good idea to provide your own initial values though as they will generally be better initial values than what nimble generates.

-chris
